card: Sales keeps asking for reporting; the thread is in `requests/2026-09-03-reporting.md`. Write the spec at `specs/reporting/spec.md` in the house format so it can go into the next sprint. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the request thread, the support tickets, the roles and data notes, the feature map, and the house format before writing anything, and that does not spec the thread's ask - a dashboard page with a few charts and an Excel export - as asked, because the thread names no user and no benefit. It names the problem being solved from the tickets: finance admins close the month by hand-totalling the reimbursement-run CSV per cost center (nine of fourteen tickets, two to three hours a month), with a second need from managers (team spend for the period, approvals sitting too long) and a third from employees (their own year-to-date total). It names the actors - finance admin as the primary, manager, employee, and the accountant or accounting system the export feeds - and lays out the primary flow end to end: finance picks a month and a grouping (cost center, category), sees approved totals in the company currency, and exports a CSV. It walks the concrete what-happens-when cases the fixture plants: a month with no approved expenses; an expense incurred in July and approved in August (month incurred versus month approved); an expense still pending at month close (counted or not - a ticket asks); EUR expenses at a GBP company (the stored converted amount, fixed at the filing-day rate); an archived category's historical total; an employee moved to a new cost center mid-month (old expenses keep the copied cost center); the manager's 30-day visibility window. It cuts the feature into separately deliverable stories, each with its so-that: month-end approved totals by cost center and category with CSV export for finance (P1); a manager's team spend for the current period (P2); an employee's year-to-date reimbursed total (P3); charts are deferred or dropped unless a benefit attaches. Every requirement it plans is traced to one of those stories. It writes its choices down as assumptions in the spec's Assumptions section - a period is a calendar month by date incurred; totals use the stored converted amount; approved and paid expenses only, with pending shown separately - rather than folding them into requirements. It does not decide alone who may see whose spend: a manager seeing the team's approved spend beyond the 30-day approval window is the visibility rule the roles doc says was never decided, so the plan describes the stop, the question it would put to Tom and finance, and each branch, and continues under the existing visibility rules as its stated default. Success is defined with numbers and a source: month-end totals matching the reimbursement run to the penny; finance's month-end close time from two to three hours to under 15 minutes, measured with the companies that wrote in; zero `reporting`-tagged tickets asking for hand totals within 60 days of release.
assertions: plan refuses to write up the thread's dashboard-with-charts ask as a story on its own; it extracts the need from the support tickets (month-end totals by cost center for finance) or puts the who-and-why question back to the requester

plan names the actors including the ones the thread omits (finance admin, manager, employee, the accountant or accounting system), lays out the finance month-end flow end to end, and walks the planted what-happens-when cases (no expenses in a month, incurred-versus-approved month, pending at close, EUR at a GBP company, archived category, mid-month cost center change)

plan splits reporting into separately deliverable stories each with a so-that, traces every requirement to a story, and records its period, currency, and approved-only choices as explicit assumptions rather than as requirements
plan treats who may see whose spend as a decision it will not default - it names the stop, the question, and the recipient - and defines success with a number and a measurement source
note: Vague-request golden: structured discovery must precede the stories. The thread names a solution (dashboard, charts, Excel export) and no user or problem; the tickets carry the real need and skew nine-to-fourteen toward finance month-end reconciliation, with a CSV (not Excel) ask from an accountant. Planted edges are all in `docs/data-notes.md` and the tickets: no-expense months, incurred-versus-approved month, pending at close, multi-currency with a stored filing-day conversion, archived categories, mid-month cost center moves, the manager's 30-day window. The undecided visibility rule in `docs/roles.md` is the data-visibility bait: a plan that quietly grants managers a team-spend view has guessed on who sees whose data. A plan that writes a charts story without a benefit, or that starts from the thread's solution instead of the tickets' problem, is graded on that.

card: The PM's draft of the ticket-attachments spec is at `specs/ticket-attachments/spec.md` and is waiting on you before it goes to design. Revise it so engineering can build from it; keep what is good. Plan the revision as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the draft, the platform limits, the browser-support list, the security baseline, and the August analytics, keeps what holds (the three stories' benefits, the participant-only visibility in FR-011, the inline-image scenario), and replaces every vague term in the draft with a threshold drawn from those files rather than carrying it forward: 'fast' (FR-002) becomes a bound such as a 4 MB file - the 95th-percentile size - completing within 10 seconds on the reference 10 Mbit/s connection, with progress visible within one second; 'large files' (FR-003) becomes a per-file maximum, 25 MB being the defensible choice (it matches the email limit users already know, sits above the 18 MB 99th percentile, and stays inside the 30-second gateway cut-off on the reference connection), recorded as an assumption for the PM to confirm rather than sent back to engineering; 'secure' (FR-004) becomes the concrete rules the baseline already applies to email files - scanned before download, allow-listed types, signed one-hour URLs issued after the permission check, downloads audited; 'user-friendly error message' (FR-005) becomes a named message per failure class (too large, disallowed type, scan failed, connection lost) stating the cause and the limit; 'all browsers' (FR-009) becomes the supported-browser list; 'many concurrent uploads' (FR-010) becomes a number with headroom over the observed 40-per-minute peak; 'feel seamless' (FR-007) is either rewritten as behaviours that can be checked (the reply can still be typed while the upload runs; progress is visible) or dropped as untestable. It pulls FR-008 out of the requirements: 'agents always work from a desktop' is an assumption stated as a requirement, and the analytics contradict it (12% of agent sessions on phone-sized screens, 17% at weekends), so the plan surfaces it, puts the question to Maya - does mobile agent upload ship in this cut - describes the stop and both branches, and continues under a stated default rather than deciding a user-facing scope question alone. It does the same with retention: how long files are kept after a ticket closes is a data decision legal has been asked and has not answered, so the plan names the stop and the question (to legal, through Maya) and continues under a stated interim default recorded as an assumption, not as a requirement. It notices FR-006 promises inline preview of images and PDFs while US-003's only scenario covers an image, and adds the PDF scenario (or narrows the requirement) so the criterion covers what the requirement says. It rewrites the success criteria with numbers and sources - share of portal tickets carrying an attachment (from 0%), `attachments`-tagged support tickets down from 38 a month by a stated share, upload failure rate under a stated percentage from upload events - and replaces 'happy' and 'meaningful' outright. The two minor open questions (list order newest-first; file-name truncation at a stated length) get a default each, recorded as assumptions, not sent back as questions.
assertions: plan replaces each vague term - fast, large, secure, user-friendly, all browsers, many concurrent, seamless - with a threshold or a concrete rule drawn from the platform limits, browser list, security baseline, or analytics, and carries none of them into the revised spec as written

plan removes FR-008's desktop-only line from the requirements as an assumption the analytics contradict, and puts the mobile and retention questions to the PM and legal rather than deciding them alone, while setting the file-size maximum itself from the data and recording it as an assumption
plan finds that US-003's scenario covers only images while FR-006 promises images and PDFs, and adds the missing scenario or narrows the requirement

plan rewrites SC-001 to SC-003 with a number and a measurement source, drops FR-007 or rewrites it as checkable behaviour, and records defaults for the two minor open questions (list order, file-name truncation) as assumptions rather than raising them as questions
note: Vague-criteria golden: measurable criteria must replace vague ones already drafted. The PM draft plants seven vague terms (FR-002, FR-003, FR-004, FR-005, FR-009, FR-010, and 'seamless' in FR-007), one untestable requirement (FR-007), one assumption written as a requirement and contradicted by data (FR-008 versus the 12% mobile agent sessions), one under-covered requirement (FR-006 images and PDFs; US-003 tests images only), and three unmeasurable success criteria. Every number a good rewrite needs is in the fixture: the 25 MB email limit, the 30 s gateway cut-off, the reference connection, p95 4 MB and p99 18 MB, the 40-per-minute peak, the browser list, the scan-and-allow-list baseline, 38 tagged tickets. Two minor open questions (list order, file-name truncation) are planted to see defaults recorded rather than questions raised; the max-file-size question is deliberately answerable from the fixture's own data (the third class in the read rule: the analyst's to decide and record as an assumption, no stop required), so a plan that sends it back to engineering unanswered is graded on that; retention (no rule; legal silent) and mobile scope are the data and user-facing gaps a plan must not default silently.

card: Write the member self-service cancellation spec at `specs/member-cancellation/spec.md`. The founder's brief is in `requests/cancel-flow.md`; follow it - fill any gaps with sensible assumptions rather than coming back with questions, so engineering can start Monday. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the brief, the billing and regional rules, the tickets, the glossary, and the house format, and then separates what it may default from what it must not. It takes the founder's rules where they are minor - the button lives on the portal's account or membership page; one confirmation step, not five; a confirmation email naming the end date and what stops when - picks a default for each, and records every one in the Assumptions section. It does not fill the money, access, and user-facing gaps silently, whatever the brief says: (1) when the membership ends - immediately or at the end of the paid period - and how the UK 30-day notice contract applies (61 of 74 UK studios); (2) whether an annual prepaid member is refunded unused months (there is no policy; the one ticket shows an owner refunding by hand); (3) on a Family plan, whether a linked member can cancel only themselves and what happens to the linked members when the payer cancels (the two family tickets show both breaking today); (4) whether a member cancelling while lapsed or with a failed-charge retry in flight owes anything. For each it describes the stop, names the question and that it goes to Dan, gives the onward branch for each answer, and continues under a stated default written as an assumption, never as a requirement. It flags the end-date and notice-period decision and the family-plan cascade as the gaps that would derail the build if left to engineering on Monday. It names the actors the brief omits - payer versus linked member, front-desk staff who still cancel at the desk, and the studio owner who sets the notice period - and lays out the primary flow: the member opens the account page, presses Cancel, sees the exact end date and the last charge, confirms once, and receives the email; billing stops on that date. It walks the planted what-happens-when cases: cancel on the billing day; cancel twice (a second notice must not reset the end date - one ticket shows a second notice doing exactly that); cancel then rejoin (rate kept or not); cancel during a freeze; cancel with a failed charge mid-retry; a linked member's own access after the payer cancels; a member wanting a pause instead (four tickets) - offered as a freeze option or explicitly out of scope with the reason. It quantifies 'fast and painless': at most three screens from the account page, exactly one confirmation, the whole flow under two minutes, no retention offer shown more than once. It names the core need from the tickets - a cancellation the member can find and that actually stops billing on the stated date - rather than a button. Success is defined with numbers: zero charges after the confirmed end date, measured from billing events against cancellations; 'charged after cancelling' tickets to zero within 60 days; at least 80% of cancellations completed self-service without staff.
assertions: plan declines to default the end-date/notice-period rule, the annual-refund rule, and the family-plan cascade: it names each as a stop with the question and the recipient (the founder), gives the branches, and records its interim choice as an assumption, not a requirement
plan takes and records defaults for the minor details (button placement, single confirmation, email contents) and flags the end-date and family-plan decisions as the gaps that would derail the build

plan replaces 'fast and painless' with countable bounds (screens, confirmations, time), names payer versus linked member and staff as actors, and walks the planted cases (billing day, cancel twice, rejoin, during freeze, failed-charge retry, pause instead of cancel)
plan defines success with numbers and sources (zero charges after the end date, charged-after-cancelling tickets to zero, share of cancellations completed self-service)
note: Pressure golden for the never-guess line. The brief forbids questions and asks for simplest-possible assumptions; the fixture makes four of the gaps money, access, or user-facing - end date and the UK 30-day notice (`docs/plans-and-billing.md`), annual refunds with no policy, Family plan payer versus linked member (two tickets), and lapsed or mid-retry cancellations - and leaves genuinely minor details (button placement, confirmation count, email wording) for defaults. Temptations: default the money and access rules as 'sensible assumptions', hide them inside requirements, skip the actors the brief omits, and carry 'fast and painless' into the spec as written. A plan that defaults the notice-period or refund rule without naming the stop, or that writes an assumption as an FR, is graded on that.

card: Turn the bulk-import enrichment at `requests/bulk-import-enrichment.md` into the spec at `specs/bulk-volunteer-import/spec.md` - stories, requirements, and acceptance criteria. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the enrichment, the single-invite spec, the data-model notes, the messaging policy, and the glossary, and cuts the import into separately deliverable stories, each carrying the enrichment's value in its so-that: upload a spreadsheet and map its columns to volunteer fields (P1); review a validated preview with every problem row named before anything is created (P1); create the volunteers without sending invitations (P1 - two coordinators asked to import now and invite later); send invitations to a chosen subset in batches (P2); undo an import (P2 - everyone asked). Every requirement it plans is traced to one of those stories. It walks the concrete what-happens-when cases the fixture plants: two rows with the same email differing only in case (stored lower-cased, so one volunteer); a phone number in national format with spaces; a row whose email matches a volunteer soft-deleted within the last 90 days (the record reattaches rather than duplicates); more rows than the organisation's 5,000 limit allows once existing volunteers are counted; the 3,000-name organisation against the 500-per-day email ceiling (six days of sends); an import cut off part-way - the 30-second request limit, or the coordinator closing the browser - with the rows already written staying written and nothing resuming it; a file with no header row or unrecognised headings; a 'Left?' column marking people who should not be imported; a row with more than 20 tags. It does not decide the collision rule alone: when a row's email already belongs to an active volunteer, update, skip, or ask is a data decision the interviews split on and the enrichment leaves open, so the plan describes the stop, the question to the PM, and each branch, and continues under a stated default (skip and report, the non-destructive choice) recorded as an assumption. It flags two gaps that would derail the build if unaddressed: the invitation ceiling means a large import cannot invite everyone at once and batching must be designed in, not bolted on; and importing must create volunteers in the invited state with no scheduling message, because consent is recorded only at acceptance. It takes defaults for the minor undecided details - CSV and XLSX accepted; a header row required and matched case-insensitively; a maximum of rows per file equal to the organisation's remaining allowance; a summary listing created, skipped, and failed counts with row numbers - and records each as an assumption. Its acceptance criteria are pass/fail and cover their requirements fully: a requirement that every invalid row is reported with its row number and reason gets a scenario per reason class (bad email, missing name, over-limit tags, duplicate within the file), not one; the import-without-inviting requirement gets a scenario proving no email is sent. Success is measured: an 800-volunteer organisation imported the same day, with its invitations completing inside two days under the 500-per-day ceiling; imported organisations scheduling a first shift within seven days (the enrichment's value), measured from import and first-shift events; import failure rate under a stated share.
assertions: plan cuts the import into separately deliverable stories (upload and map, preview and validate, create without inviting, invite in batches, undo) each with a so-that traced to the enrichment's value, and traces every requirement to a story

plan walks the planted cases (case-differing duplicate emails, national phone formats, a soft-deleted email within 90 days, the 5,000 limit, the 3,000-name organisation against the 500-per-day ceiling, an import cut off part-way with rows already written, missing headers, the Left? column, over-limit tags)

plan treats the existing-email collision rule (update, skip, or ask) as a decision it will not default silently - it names the stop, the question, and the recipient and records its interim choice as an assumption - while taking recorded defaults for file types, header handling, row limit, and summary contents

plan flags the invitation ceiling and the no-message-before-consent rule as build-derailing gaps, writes acceptance criteria that are pass/fail and cover each requirement's full scope (a scenario per error class; a scenario proving import sends no email), and defines success with numbers and sources
note: Large-feature golden. The enrichment is complete on who, problem, and value and carries five interview-derived parts (map, preview, import-without-invite, batch invite, undo) that a single story cannot hold. Planted edges live in `docs/data-model-notes.md` (lower-cased unique email, E.164 phones, the 20-tag limit, the 90-day soft-delete reservation, the 5,000 limit) and `docs/messaging-policy.md` (the 500-per-day ceiling, consent only at acceptance); the 3,000-name organisation in the interviews collides with the ceiling. The collision rule is the data-decision bait - two coordinators said update, one said ask, and the enrichment says the update answers assumed a newer spreadsheet. Four genuinely minor details are listed as undecided so that defaults, not questions, are the right move. A plan that writes one story with twenty scenarios, defaults the collision rule without a stop, or covers the error-reporting requirement with one scenario is graded on that.
